The London Morning Post thus explains the ill success of the English in their attack on the llcdan : þÿ The Malakoff Tower is, as is well known, the highest point of the fortifications which defended Sebustopol. It is flanked on cither side by the Grand Redan, the object of the English attack, and the Redan of Careening Bay. Now, behind these forts the Russians had constructed a formidable second line of earthworks, heavily armed, which commanded all the works in front, with the exception of the Malakoff Tower, and this exception was due to the overcarc of the Russians, who, in their anxiety to strengthen the MalakoflF, had built its works in three tiers, the one rising abovo the other, whereas the Redans were constructed with only one tier of guns. The consequence of this was, that when the French swarmed on the first tier of the MalakoflF, the second tier saved them from being hurt by the fire of the works in the rear of the Tower ; and, in like manner, when they attained the second tier, the third saved them in its turn. Consequently, thousands of men thronged its ramparts, protected from the Russian fire. The combat raged on the flanks, where the enemy could only attack them with his musketry, and their own rifles and brilliant impetuosity were too much for him. Under the protection of a galling fire from the French, their sappers slipped round the work, threw up an entrenchment, and thus, effectually covered on all points, the whole work was theirs. Here, then, to brave men success was as natural

as their own enthusiastic courage ; but, alas ' upon other points courage availed not. The gallant assailants of the Redan and of the Central Bastion no sooner had carried these works, as they did triumphantly, than they found themselves exposed to a terrific close fire of grape, V in one exposed tier, wore open to the full range which rendered life impossible. The forts, built of the second line of earthworks, and in vain our gallant men, in vain our chivalrous Allies, tried to hold their position. They would not retreat, but were swept away as corpses by the pitiless storm of grape. The tenacity of our struggle may be easily conceived when it is known that in carrying, and in endeavouring to hold, that men one Redan, our loss amounted to two thousand "

Is all civilized communities the Press is generally considered the palladium for the diffusion of useful knowledge, and the channel through which the peasant as well as the prince may of the people's rights, and " a terror to evil speak. It is likewise the most powerful organ doers." But how can such an instrument operate fully when shackled ; we adopt the term because we view the tax on newspapers in no lesser þÿlight for without free circulation the river becomes a pool, so also the press becomes a dead letter. A celebrated author Montesquieu þÿ emphatically says, " where there is a press, you are sure of liberty." The quotation is appropriate, and marked with a degree of meaning, which cannot be well misunderstood. In the concluding part of an article from the pen of the Editor of the Trinidad Reporter , we find the following cogent remarks : þÿ " The proprietors of the press cannot be expected to bear the very heavy tax. It is a question which should interest the community, and they ought to take the subject in hand. We have thrown out these observations, as we are but just established, wr should like to know the opinions of our contemporaries on the subject, and what steps they intend to adopt. The matter cannot lie at rest. The injustice is too glaring, and we think that the respective communities should appeal to Parliament. It they arc wanting in their duty, let the whole responsibility devolve upon the Press, and thev will perform their duty we trust nobly and ef-
fectually " We give the article in ertenso on our fourth page.

TREATMENT of the YELLOW FEVER. Captain Jones P. Levy, late of the United States transport-ship American, who has had ! hundreds of cases of Yellow Fever under treatment, says he never knew of a case terminating fatally after observing the following directions : þÿ " Dissolve in a wine glass of water a table spoonfull of common salt, and pour the same into a tumbler, adding the juice of a whole lemon, and two wine glasses of castor oil. The whole to be taken at one dose (by an adult) ; then a hot mustard foot bath, with a handful of salt in the water ; the patient to be well wrapped in blankets until perspiration takes place freely. On removal to bed the feet of the patient is to be wrapped in the blanket þÿ afterwards apply mus- , tard plasters to the abdomen, legs, and soles of rapidly full, even so small an amount as one ' the feet. If the headache is very acute, apply I mustard plasters to the head and temples. After the fever has been broken, take forty grains I of quinine and forty drops elixir of vitriol to a of j quart of water. Dose þÿ wine glass full three times a day. Barley water, lemonade, and ice water, may be used in moderation. þÿ St. Thomas Times.

We have had only two square-rigged vessels enter the port I tions of an approaching huriicane may up during the week, a circumstance which may-be affords no parelle! in St. Thomas affairs þÿ the very rare calms that have prevailed during the l ist ten days. Our harbor at the present time only boasts of about twelve vessel < þÿ including large and j small þÿ discouraging enough to look at, and might lead us to despond, were it not that we know it is only incidental to the season, and as we are just passing over the same, we hope iri another fortnight to witness that animation and movement on our waters so common during nine months of the year. likely have arrived but for the calms alluded to ; each of these are coming richly freighted with Europe's merchandize, and the warehouses of this place will shortly exhibit that bulk and

It was by labour that all the men who are now great in history for their civil words and noble deeds, who wrote books, built cathedrals, made laws, and governed people, succeeded. Let no body think honourable labour a hardship ; rather let him regard it as a necessity, a duty, an enjoyment, and the true secret of success in life. The late Rev. Rowland Hill was asked a long life, and he said Hard works." which were the best means of securing " Labour not only contributes to the length of life, but makes it useful. 3 T a A T I 8, THE POSTAGE ON NEWSPAPERS. From the Trinidad "Reporter."

We have received 8 colonial papers in all by the Packet, we presume in consequence of the Postage fee payable in advance on Colonial Newspapers. Before the passing of the late act, Colonial Papers came free ; now we must pay for each paper one penny. In England the question of stamps upon Newspapers had engaged attention very much, and the subject was brought before Parliament ; it was very ably and successfully argued. The effect of repealing the stamp duty in England has been to enable the proprietors to lower the prices of their papers ; a measure which is calculated to be of very material importance in securing the pre-eminence of the Press. Its effect upon the Colonies, to make them pay a portion of the duties which were levied under the stamp act. We consider the measure as extremely unfair and ungenerous towards the Colonies. The imposition of the stamp duty was a tax on knowledge, and it impeded the free circulation of the papers. The very same arguments which were so successfully urged in England, could with equal, if not greater, propriety (viewing our circumstance) bo urged here. We calculate that it will be a tax on the Colonies of not less than £850 to £900 a-year. We receive by every Packet about 80 Colonial papers, and forward about 65 ; and we are placed in this position, either to suffer an annual loss of about £10 if we continue to send our papers : (while our contemporaries forwarding their papers, must bear some the same loss, and others double) or to raise the price of our

subscription to cover the extra expense. In the first place it is essentially important that the exchange of files should be kept up with our contemporaries. For various reasons we should know and the public be acquainted with the leading events which occur. It were a mere waste of time to point out the benefits which we derive from the exchange of files. On the other hand, to bo enabled still to keep up our communication with the Colonics, we must increase the price of the Paper. In Trinidad above all places, every fucility should be afforded to the circulation of papers, as a means cheap aud speedy of communicating intelligence and political events to everybody ; and a source of regret to us it is, that our island papers cannot be lessened in price. In such an event then, and presuming that our contemporaries would follow the same course, the respective communities would be taxed between them some £900. We can only speak of Trinidad ; and we look upon an increase of subscription as a death blow to political Independence. The matter is more important than at first sight appears. The people are not in a position to pay any increased price, and as we suppose in the Colonies there are numbers of persons who subscribe to two newspapers, the tax upon those will be doubled. Increase the price of the paper, the press perhaps no longer exists. The proprietors of the press cannot be expected to bear the very heavy tax It is a question which should interest the community, and they ought to take the

subject in hand. We have thrown out these observations, as we are but just established, we should like to know the opinions of our contemporaries on the subject, and what steps they intend to adopt. The matter cannot lie at rest. The injustice is too glaring, and we think that the respective communities should appeal to Parliament. If they are wanting in their duty, let the whole responsibility devolve upon the Press, and they will perform their duty we trust nobly aud effectually
PROSPECTS OF THE RUSSIAN ARMY IN THE CRIMEA From the London Times.

The struggle for the possession of Sebnstopol is at an end. That prize is in our hands, and. as the defence of the fortress and the harbour was the grand object of the Russians, they have nothing left on that spot to contend for. The mere occupation of the northe side of the port is a barren advantage, for, though it might hold a garrison, it cannot shelter a defeated army ; and it is obvious that, after the failure of the main object, al' the ability of the generalship of the Russians will be required to withdraw the body of their forces in the Crimea from desl ruction, and we, therefore, infer that the north em 'oris will either be held for a time by a limited garrison, or, more probably altogether abandoned, in the hope of saving the army. Never was an army in a more critical position. They are confined within a peninsula which affords them no other fortified position, no sustenance for the troops, and no water beyond a certain line. The sea, covered with hostile vessels, surrounds three sides of this theatre of war, and the fourth is separated from the Russian base of opciations bysteppes and marshes. The Allied armies already occupy strong positions at Eupatoria and Yenikale, which can be reinforced in a few hours by sea, so as to threaten the Russians in their flank and rear ; and while it is impossible for the enemy to hold his ground in the south of the Crimea þÿ for which, indeed, there is now no further object þÿ to retreat in this season across the country is a formidable

undertaking, while the loss of a battle in the open field would be absolute destruction. The Russians are in a trap, from which the Tchongar road and the Isthmus of Perckop are the only means of escape, and even there their communications may possibly be intercepted.

ENGLAND'S DECLINE. Those who talk about England's decline, and fix her position as a second or third rate Power, because she lias lost 30,000 men before Sebastopol. talk twaddle. The loss of ten such armies would only serve to unveil her resources, and bring out the indomitable energy of her people. She is a maritime Power. Her commerce establishes her rank among nations ; and her navy is strong enough to foster, guard, and watch over tliat commerce in every quarter of the globe. When the first shows symptoms of decay, or the latter is powerless to protect, then, and not till then, will Great Britain lose her prestige, and fall from the 'ofty position she has for centuries occupied. þÿ New York Times. Al Alb ! IViiut is it f Oi'R present stock of intelligence þÿ European and Colonial þÿ is about exhausted ; but just in time to be replenished for Tuesday's issue. 'Tis true the tables in our sanctum now groan under the weight of newspapers and periodicals of every description, but, these contain not a whit of politics that could in any wise interest or concern the local or distant reader ; therefore do we look forward with lively interest to the Atrato's arrival from Europe, as by that ship we may hope to learn of further successes having crowned the eflorts of the Allied Arms in the Crimea, and the likelihood of Peace being speedily restored to all Europe ! War is a curse and a blessing ! A curse in the destruction of human þÿlife a blessing for the strong arm it wields in favor of civilization over barbarism ! Father fighting against son, son against father, and brother against þÿbrother such is bloody War. But without this, the World would lose its equilibrium, We could not pass over the sentiments of a writer in the Christian Intelligencer, which wo copy in part from a contemporary, without feeling the truthfulness of them : þÿ " War is what people coolly talk about, as if it were a holyday pastime ! This is what men array themselves in gold and plumage for, and go out too with drums beating, and colours flying ! This is what men rejoice over in cathedrals, and

offer up thanksgiving to Him whom they called the God of Battles 1" Spirit of the benevo- " lent Jesus ! is this the religion thou didst come to teach ? " As for myself, whenever I read a highsounding bulletin of victory, I never can fix my mind upon it. It wanders away to that hospital where the wounded victims are breathing out their lives in agony. It wanders to the cottagifireside, where sits the lone widow, mourniug. like Rachael, and " will not be comforted where the lisping child asks when his father will come back, and is þÿtold what his young heart is slow to þÿunderstand that some strange man met his father on the battle-field, and smote him to the earth ! My mind wanders up to that gathering, so suddeu, so awful, before the Throne of God "and 1 ask mysell when will this stupenduous system of havoc and of blood be swept from the face of indignant earth ; Even now, while the armies of Europe are mustering for conflict, shall not all Christians unite their prayers to God that national wrongs may be righted, and that the interests of justice and freedom he secured without the terrific necessity of War 1 Let the old armour rust ! Let us try the new armour ot Truth, and Justice, and Love."

DANCING. þÿ De Quincey, speaking of Dancing, says in one of his essays, " And in itself, of all the scenes which this world offers, none is to me so profoundly interesting, none ( I say deliberately) so affecting as the spectacle of men and women floating through the mazes of a dance ; under these conditions, however, that the music shall be rich and festal, the execution of the dancers perfect, and the dance itself of a character to admit of free, fluent, and continuous motion. And whenever the music happens to be not of a light, trivial character, but charged with the spirit of festal pleasure, and the performers in the dance so far skilful as to betray no awkwardness verging on the ludicrous, I believe that many persons feel as 1 feci in such circumstances, namely, derive from the spectacle the very grandest form of passionate sadness which can belong to any spectacle whatsoever." The same writer goes on to remark : þÿ " 'The reason is in part, that such a scene presents a sort of mask of human life, with its whole equipage of pomps and glories, its luxuries of sight and sound, its hours i>i' golden youth, and the interminable revolution i of ages liurryiug after ages, and one generation treading over the flying footsteps of another, while all the while the overruling music attempers the mind to the spectacle, the subject (as a German would say) to the object, the beholder to the vision."

Each of the three Islands St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. Johns, and their dependencies, shall as hiherto 8, in St. Thomas ofG, and in St. Johns of 3 members ministration of the Superior Authority, with excep- for the same, under the inspection and superior ad- tion of those matters regarding which special regu- nistration appertains to the Burgher Council elected lations have been directed. lie a separate municipality, whose economical admi- The Burgher Council shall consist in St. Croix of . 2who are to be elected according to the rules contained in this ordinance. 3 Qualified to vote is every man of unblemished character who has attained the age of 25 years, and is not subject to legal incapacity, and a, eitherhas a burgherbrief in the Island, and can prove that he has an annual income of $500, or pays at least $5 annual ground-and building-tax to the State-Treasury of a property in the Island belonging to himself, or leased to him by recorded contract for a term of at least 5 years, or in St. Thomas pays at least $12 annual trade-or store-tax to the Land-Treasury ; b, or without regard to his having a burgherbrief or

If any such property as above stated is possessed by several persons jointly, the right to vote can only be exercised by one of them whom the others have authorized to exercise it, provided that he possesses the other qualifications required. 4. Qualified to be elected, is every person entitled to vote who pays at least $8 annual ground-and building-tax to the State-Treasury of a property in the Island, and subject to the rules contained in 3 relative to a lease for several years or to the joint possession of a property, þÿ or in St. Thomas pays at least $40 annual trade-or store-tax to the Land-Treasury. It is besides requisite that he is domiciled in the Island, and must have resided there at least one year before he can he elected. 5. No person can enter a Burgher Council when hc is related, or in affinity in the ascending or descending lineage or in the first degree of the collateral line, to a member already elected, but subsequent affinity shall not cause any withdrawal. In commercial firms only one partner can be member of the Burgher Council. If two persons related as above are elected at the same time, only the one, who has the plurality of votes shall be member, and if they have an equal number of votes, drawing of lots shall decide which of them it shall be ; the other to be considered as not elected 6. The members of the Burgher Council are elected

by plurality of votes, and have to officiate 4 years in St. Croix, and 3 years in the other Islands. After the publication of this ordinance a general election of ail the members of the Burgher Councils shall take place. At the expiration of each succeeding year two members for St. Croix and for St. Thomas, and one for St. Johns will have to resign, and a new election of an equal number of members is to take place.

AT 13, In regard to which of the members, simultaneously elected, will have to resign, this must be decided by mutual agreement or in default of this by drawing of lots ; otherwise it is the rule, that those members whose election is of the oldest date, retire first. The members retiring may be re-elected. If a vacancy occur during the course of the year, a new member is to be elected. The new election, on account of a vacancy occurring during the last three months of the year may however be postponed until the regular election at the expiration of the year is to take place, provided that circumstances, according to the opinion of the Superior Authority or the Burgher Council, do not demand that the vacant seat be filled previously. The person elected in lieu of a retiring member has only to serve for the remaining period for which the retiring member was elected. The regular yearly elections ought to take place so early that the result may be published within the expiration of the year, and the term of service to be reckoned from the 1st of January. In the particular case mentioned below in 14 where an entirely new Burgher Council has to be elected, the members of this have to retire in the same manner as the members elected at the first general election after the publication of this ordinance.

7. The Island of St. Croix shall constitute 2 elective districts according to the jurisdictions, that of Christiansted electing 5 and that of Frederiksted 3 members. The Islands of St. Thomas and St. Johns constitute each an elective district. The judges in the three towns and in St. Johns, each in his jurisdiction, have to conduct the elections as directors. The Burgher Council concerned prepares yearly a list of all those qualified to vote in the Island, and another list of those who can be elected, with statement of their full names alphabetically arranged, their vocation and abode. When the lists are completed, they are to be exhibited in a proper place for 14 days, notice thereof to be given previously. 8.

If any person unqualified to vote or to be elected has been entered in the lists, or any person has been omitted in the same, any one may represent the case to the director of the elections in the jurisdiction where the concerned resides, by stating in writing the fact with reference to arguments and proofs within 3 days from the expiration of the time in which the lists are exhibited for inspection. The objections or remarks thus made against the lists, are to be decided upon by the electoral Committee, consisting of the director, a member of the Burgher Council, and another trustworthy person appointed by the Burgher Council for that purpose, in a public meeting to be held in the course of the following 8 days. The persons who have made such remarks, as well as those against whom objections have been made, are to be summoned to said meeting, and a copy of the statement containing the objections to be delivered to the concerned. If the decision has an influence on the qualification of any person to be elected or not the result must be published in a proper manner. In case of an election during the course of the year, the lists already made are to be used, without being again publicly exhibited.

$ 9. The day for the public election is to be fixed by the directors respectively. In St. Croix the election ought to take place on the same day in both jurisdictions, and the electors may vote on any citizen qualified to be elected without regard to whether he resides in the one or the other jurisdiction. The directors shall at least 8 days previous to the election, publish in the usual manner, the place where the election is to be held, and likewise the day, and the hour when it is to commence and when it is to be closed; furthermore the names of the retiring members are to be mentioned.

THE STEREOSCOPE \\ e live in an age of wonderful improvement. This curious optical apparatus is becoming daily more interesting and valuable. The facilities afforded by the daguerreotype of taking views of the same object according to the varying angles of the two eyes þÿ which is illustrative of the theory of double vision þÿ has provided the stereoscope with inexhaustible subjects, and the pictures which have been produced by English and other Photographers arc said to be among the most beautiful specimens of any known process. Those who are unfamiliar with the stereoscope, and it.- relation to the photographic art, can have little idea how exquisitely the sense of relief resident in natural vision is realised by the artificial media of two pictures surveyed through a divided lens, which has the effect of uniting the two perspectives, and endowing the flat surfaces under the eye, as it were, with a tangible solidity. I he launch in England of the Marlborough may

3 tl\ Q ift D it T Jt 3 also afford another proof of the miraculous process of the Stereoscope. The paper before us says : þÿ " By especial command of her Majesty, M. T. R. Williams, of Regent-street, was commissioned to take a series of stereoscopic views of the launch of the Marlborough. 1 laving been favored with an opportunity of examining the results, we emphatically declare them to be the most successful instantaneous photographs that we have yet seen. The operations, indeed, must have been literally as quick as lightning, for the surf which crested the waves, the spray thrown from the paddle-wheels of the steamers, the rowers in the craft which studded the water, the puffs of vapour from the steam funnels, and the balls of cloud from the guns of the Illustrious, are indicated with a sharpness and individuality of detail that might fairly have been thought impossible. The beauty, indeed, of these views is unsurpassable, considered simply as photographic efforts, without reference to the disturbing conditions to the operators of the entire scene and its accessories being more or less in motion. With such photographic issue as those before our eyes, it is evident that future generations will not be without pictorial records of historical events of the highest interest and importance, however evanescent may be their practical existence."

Pop goes the Question. þÿ " Pop goes the question," has often led people a very pretty dance. It has been a pop that has always been exeedingly popular, and is revived from time to time, as much from necessity as fashion. The step is a very decided one ; but though usually regarded as difficult,

yet a little boldness and address is all that is required to make the gentleman a rapid proficient. þÿ The steps are taken as follows: þÿ Gentleman hows to lady; chassee to lady's side ; hands across ; halancez, and set (on a chair). Lady (makes) advances, and retreats (into herself) gentleman follows up (his advantage,) and halancez (on the chair) ; lady's chain (of endearments) cavalier seu I ; set (to work) ; right and left small talk ; heads round with excitement ; down the middle and up again with prepared speeches ; gentleman takes lady's hand ; lady withdraws it; pousctte; right and left; hands across; gentleman drops on one knee, and turns the lady to his purpose ; grand round of arm about the waist þÿ Pop goes the question ! This step is generally concluded by the figures joining hands and uniting in a ring. The usual finale to the step is childish in the extreme.

It is possible his assertions may be exaggerated ; but, at any rate, now that the allies have done so much towards becoming masters of the Crimea, such a subject is extremely interesting. If England and France were to take possession of the whole of the Crimea, and wished, without keeping up on army of occupation at a vast expense, to prevent Russia from ever re-establishing her power, they have only to decree that henceforward the Crimea should be an independent Slate, selfgoverned. And to attract thither in less than a year as many millions of inhabitants as could be lodged or, the soil, it would be þÿsufli nient for them to declare lite ports free, and to plant on the summit of the Tchatir Dngli, a banner inviting the gold-seekers of every nation to come and search its sides. In the rocks of lite Tchatir, the Dimirdgi, Sinab and Aluchts, there is enough to pay the expenses of a war if it lasted a century. Perhaps my readers may feel astonished at my making such a statement ; they would be no less astonished if they knew the authorities on which 1 rely. I do not merely appeal to geographical documents and the history of past limes to prove infallibly that the gold mines of the Tehatir Dagh exist and have been worked; I also invoke the testimony of those who, de visu, de tnanu have seen and touched veins of gold more abundant, a

thousand- fold richer than Ikose of the Ural and all the known mines. It suited the policy of the Czars to leave these mines unworkcd, and to efface the recollections of them as far as possible. If they were worked by free men, that would have attracted from every corner of Europe a multitude of adventurers, men of an enterprising character on a single point of the empire; it would have been kindling a conflagration which they could not have mastered. If, on the other hand, serfs and prisoners were employed as miners, the Crimea was not, like the Ural, so remote from Europe that the groans of the slave mart) rs could be smothered, and they might have escaped from the fangs of the despot. The Russian Government, consequently, proclaims tho auriferous

strata of these mountains, which evidently attach the Alps the Caucasus, to be fabu- to lous. In the time of the Argonauts, a portion of the golden fleece was drying on the Tent Mountain. The Romans and Greeks, and above all Mithridates, helped themselves. The Tartars, the Mongols, nomadic and pastoral tiibes, despised gold as useless; but the Genoese, following the example of the Eastern emperors, mysteriously worked these inexhaustible riches ; and not to arouse the cupidity of their rivals, the Venetians, the Catalans, the Pisarts, and (lie Barons of the Holy Land, they pretended that all the gold they imported into Europe was obtained by the commerce with the East Indies, which then followed the land route. Baron de Tott, whom the Court of Versailles sent as Ambassador to the Krim Guerai, alludes in his Memoirs" to the unexplored mines of " the Tchatir Dagh, and asserts that the Khan of the Crimea does not work them for fear of exciting the cupidity of the Padishah of Constantinople, his suzerain. Our good friends the English have already turned their eyes on this Eastern California, and you may be certain that they will benefit by it first of all. The Crimea, within ten years, wijl become the El Dorado of the Old World.

This sacred Edifice presented an imposing and a very crowded appearance last evening, in answer to the invitation of the Rector to attend the second reading of his Sermon on " Marriage, and the evils arising from its neglect in the community." The evils pointed out by the reverend gentleman are legion ; and, we are pained to say, are fearfully extending instead of decreasing. It is full time, then, to speak out loudly and plainly ; and our only wonder is that the Pulpit should have remained so long silent. Nothing, we believe, but. a false delicacy prevented our Clergymen from grappling with the difficulties of the subject. But an evil to be removed, must be known. The policy of silence then þÿ of affected horror, of conventional suppression of all open reference, either spoken or written, in such matters, is either cowardly, or cruel, or both, while the evils themselves are spreading their ravages, and doing their work of death and ruin in secret. Somebody must break through the trammels of false delicacy, and impart instruction on such vital matters. No fear of offending the overdelicate should deter from an exposure of these evils. We know that there are many whose sensibilities are so very delicate that, like the soft Sybarite, they cannot bear the rustling of a rose-leaf. Alas ! there is too much reason to fear that this affected purity is less based on the modesty of virtue than on the consciousness of guilt. Therefore do we hope that the work of wholesome reproof and advice, only
commenced, may not be allowed to cease until all are brought to the knowledge of the eternal welfare of themselves and þÿfellow-beings. «' Let them Marry.'1''

FULL RETREAT OF THE RUSSIANS ! This famous Ship reached St. Thomas on Tuesday morning, the 16th. Our packet letters wore landed here early yesterday from the Vigilant. They wero dispatched from St. Thomas on Tuesday afternoon or noon by the sloop having overtaken the sloop " on the road" took Industry ; the schooner left subsequently, and the mails from her, and caused them to be landed here four or five hours earlier than if they bad been kept on board the former vessel. The Atrato conveys full details of the bombardment and capture of Sebastopol. It is said that Prince Gortschakoff does not intend to surrender the Northern forts without a determined struggle ; on the other hand it is asserted that his retreat had already begun. It is added that the Czar has gone by the way of Moscow and Nicolaieff to the Crimea, and many regiments of troops are still being poured in that direction-

Intelligence had reached England from St. Petersburg, by way of Brussels, and is contained in a despatch from Prince Gortschakoff to his Royal Master, that a reinforcement of 30,000 men of the Allied troops had been sent to Eupatoria, had landed there, had attacked and defeated the Russians, who were compelled to "retire over the heights of Rusta." The (Jester reichiscli Zeitung announces that the bombardment of the North Forts of Sebastopol began on the 29th ultimo (September), that the Russian army was in full retreat, and that it had reached Akak, three days march from Mackenzie's Farm. This intelligence respecting the retreat must be received with extreme caution.

THE PRIME A. Sebastopol, Sep. 16. The Russians are fortifying the North part, and are constructing new batteries. The Allies are advancing cavalry and a column of infantry towards Bakshiserai by the Baudar road. Sebastopol is to be razed, and the basins filled up. Sebastopol, Sep. 18. The enemy is firing into the town. The siege batteries arc being resbipped. Vienna, Sep. 29. The Allied Fleets have left Sebastopol Their destination is unknown.

THE ALLIED ARMY IN THE CRIMEA. St. Petersburg, Sep. 26. Prince Gortschakoff reports, under date the 23rd instant, that the enemy has landed 20,000 men at Eupatoria, and the Allies have now 30, 000 men on our flank. Yesterday they attacked our infantry, who retreated to the heights over Rusta.

RUSSIA. The intelligence received from St. Petersburg is to the effect that Russia is preparing to continue the war in the most energetic manner. The Emperor is himself going to the seat of war. It is stated that, on receiving the news of the fall of Scbastopol, he exclaimed, " Better that not a single tile should be left on the roofs in St Petersburg, than that we should lose a single inch in the Crimea." At St. Petersburg they have no belief in peace ; they say that the intercessions of Prussia and Austria have been fruitless. They see that England is detested far more at St. Petersburg than France. They would be very willing to be on good terms with Franco, but they are convinced that the old system of dividing England and þÿFrance a system to which Russia owes all her influence þÿ is no longer applicable.

AT1! 3 Germany, makes the following comments on the fall of Sebastopol : Sebastopol has fallen þÿ fallen after a struggle which has not its equal in the history of wars þÿ but yet fallen, and we have to consider the importance of this event, its certain and probable consequences, for it might happen that a more earnest and pressing warning than ever might be given to Germany to exchange its present neutrality for a position which, if it does not place the decision in its hands, would at least make it participate therein. Sebastopol fell as it was doomed to fall, and when the JYord endeavors to demonstrate that it is only now that the army is concentrated in the Northern forts, that there is unity in its action and movements, it is comically absurd. We do not wish to overrate the event of the 8th of September, but we must not underrate it. The Northern fortress may be a stronger, a much stronger fortress ; but the South part contained everything which Sebastopol had to defend þÿ the whole of Russia's Black Sea fleet, and all the resources of that fleet. All this is annihilated ; and for at least half a century to come, even without the stipulations of a peace, through the simple force of circumstances, the limitation of the naval power of Russia is an accomplished fact. The third guarantee point no longer exists. But there is a point of still greater importance. The prestige of Russia's inviolability is gone þÿ gone in the East as in the West ; her whole power is shaken to its centre, and this es-

pecially because Sebastopol did not fall at once, and because it has only fallen now. It would be superflous now to investigate whether it was possible or impossible to have taken the fortress by a coup de main immediately after landing in the Crimea ; but then Sebastopol would only have been taken, and Sebastopol is not the Crimea, much less Russia. But since then every nerve has been strained to keep the place. Russia has fought in vain, and an incongruous host, with no other retreat than the sea, has beaten their army on its own ground, with an immense empire behind it, and when the highest stake was played for the position of Russia in the East.

3 IT ORDINANCE concerning tlic Burgher-Councils in the Danish West-India Possessions. WE FKEDERIK the SEVENTH, By the grace of God King of Denmark, (he Vandals and the Goths, Duke of Sleswick, llolsteen, Stormarn, Ditmarsh, Lauenhorg and Oldenborg, Make known : On the report of Our Minister of Finance who has laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council on a Draft of a Municipal Ordinance for Our Danish West-India Possessions, We most graciously decree : $ 10. The electoral Committee has to meet at the place of the election on the day and hour appointed, and to produce there the lists for the whole Island, with the additional corrections, if such have taken place according to $8. The director has to declare the meeting opened, and to take care that the election proceeds in due order. Every person who will exercise his right of voting must appear personally at the place of election. In giving his votes, he has to mention as many persons as are to be elected in his district (see 6), stating their names and vocation. The votes are to be registered in two protocols, one in charge of each of the assistants of the director; in the one is to be entered the name of each voter, and next to it the names of those persons he votes for, but in the other the names of those voted for, and under each of them the names of the voters. The minutes to be read to the voter, verified by him and compared together. When no more persons qualified to vote are desirous to take part in the election, to which access

shall be had at least for 4 hours, the members of the electoral Committee will then enter their own votes. The voting being finished the votes are to be added up, and in St. Croix the two electoral Committees have to give each other notice of the result of the election, and the persons who have attained the greatest number of votes are thereafter to be declared members of the Burgher Council. If two or more persons have an equal number of votes, the result is to be decided by drawing of lots by the chairman. " Those who have been elected will receive a written communication of their election from the director, who at the same time has to report the result of the election to the Superior Authority. If the person elected wishes to be exempted, the Burgher Council will have to decide whether the cause assigned can be considered sufficient. Any person having obtained the age of 60 years or who in the last 3 years has been member of the Burgher Council and officiated as such for at least 3 years, has a right to decline to accept the election. The same is applicable to all public functionaries. The Governor and the Government-Secretary, the President and the Secretary at St. Thomas, are according to their position not eligible. Each Burgher Council decides the validity of the election of its members. 12. The person elected memberol the Burgher Council, shall transmit to the Superior Authority a declaration in writing, binding himself on oath to perform with conscientious fidelity the duties incumbent on

him in that capacity. Such a declaration on oath once given is to be considered binding for a member re-elected after the expiration of his term. The members of the Burgher Council as long as they officiate are entitled to be exempted from all similar personal charges as a burgher. $ 13. If any person who has been elected member of the Burgher Council, in the course of the time in which he has to officiate, should become subject to any of those events which deprive him of the capacity required to perform said function, he is to be dismissed ; however it is to be observed, that the circumstance, that the amount of ground-and building-tax or of trade-or-store-tax assessed on any member, has since been reduced beneath the amount prescribed in $4, shall riot cause his withdrawal. Absence from the Island for a longer period than 2 months, or any other temporary impediment which lasts beyond said period shall also involve the resignation of the concerned. It devolves on the Superior Authority to whom the Burgher Council in each case has to give a report, founded on facts, to decide the questions which may arise in the abovementioned cases, or when any member of the Burgher Council has committed such transgressions of duty which make his dismissal necessary. $ 14. Should it happen, contrary to expectation, that the Burgher Council was found repeatedly setting aside

AT 113. its duties, and the circumstances at the same time were such as not to allow to await of Our own Resolution, the Governor then is authorized to dissolve the Burgher Council, and to cause new members to be elected, and to suspend the future eligibility of the guilty persons for a space of time equal to the term fixed for officiating as member of the Burgher Council in the Island, ($6.) The Governor provides for the performance of the current transactions, until a new election can take place. $ 15. The Burgher Council has to elect among its members a chairman, at the commencement of each year. He has to convoke the Council when required, to conduct the proceedings, and to cause the resolutions correctly entered in the protocol and dispatched. In case of an equal number of votes, the opinion to which he accedes, shall be considered as that of the majority. The Burgher Council has also to elect a vice-chairman, who has to act in the absence of the chairman. No resolution can be passed unless more than the half number of the members are present and take part in the voting. The protocol is to be signed at the close of every meeting and by all the members present. Excepting in cases of urgency, the members are to have 24 hours notice of every meeting, which has not been fixed at a previous meeting, and are to be informed of what is to be discussed in the same. Every member is entitled to demand, that any subject proposed by him be discussed in due time, and that the needful in that respect be entered in the

protocol. Each member is responsible for the acts of the Burgher Council, in case he has been present at the final discussion of the case in question and has not immediately entered his dissenting vote in the protocol. For the rest it is left to each Burgher Council to adopt the rules for their proceedings, and it may authorize individual members to decide certain cases, of which the Superior Authority must be informed. The chairman has within 14 days after each meeting to cause an extract of the proceedings of the Burgher Council published in printing. $ 16. In such cases where members of the Burgher Council or other citizens according to existing regulations, shall have a seat in Commissions for the poor, the schools or the hospitals, or in any other Commission regarding the interest of the municipality, the appointment of such persons devolves upon the Burgher Council, and a report thereof is to lie given to the Superior Authority. The Burgher Council has a right, subject to the approval of the Government to appoint t ire otficials necessary for the performance of its business, and to issue such instructions as may be required. $ 17. The revenues and expenditures of the municipality as well as the properties and other institutions belonging to the same, are, if not exempted therefrom by the existing laws, to be administered bv each Burgher Council under the inspection of the Superior Authority. When in this respect any cases occur concerning affairs under the supervision of certain

officials, such as the masters of Police or the chief inspector of roads, or entrusted to the commissions mentioned in 16, such cases may, if it be deemed proper and expedient, be referred to a mutual deliberation, verbal or in writing, of the Burgher Council and the respective officials or commissions, either by mutual agreement, previous to laying the case before the Superior Authority, or bv order of the latter. The Burgher Council may be summoned to a meeting before the Superior Authority, when the latter considers it proper to deliberate verbally on any subject, and officials or others, whose opinions or statements are desired, may be called to attenil the same meeting. It is however at the option of the Burgher Council to reserve for itself to pass its final decision in such a case in a meeting without the presence of the Superior Authority. The Burgher Council is bound to give its opinion on every matter, which the Superior Authority lays before the Burgher Council for deliberation. Furthermore We extend to all the Burgher Councils of Our Danish West-India Possessions the right granted by the ltoyal Rescript of the 8th April 1768 2 to the Burgher Council of St. Croix, in consequence of which each Burgher Council shall be entitled to make such proposals to Our Governor as are considered tending to the common interest of the municipality. to the editor of the " avis." SIR, þÿ Of all the evils under the sun, that of making irreligion commendable is the greatest. In this age we behold things for which we ought to have an abhorrence, not only received without disdain hut even valued as motives of emulation. Most of the artifice which is used among men, does not proceed from a degeneracy of nature as of an affectation of appearing men of consequence ; there is Kraal the corporal, who makes it the business of his life to be thought a clever, cunning fellow, and thinks it a greater character to be doing mischief than good to his fellow man, and is proud of the capacity of doing mischief. Tt is certain that corporal Kraal fears the imputation of want of understanding much more than the abuse of it, but alas ! how contemptible is such an ambition, which is the very reverse of all that is laudable. When the spider is ranging in the different apartments of his web it is true that he only can weave so fine a thread, but it is in the power of the merest drone that has wings, to fly through and destroy it. I have read of the history of such a character in France. In the midst of his fanatical success he fell sick, and was reclaimed to such a sense of his condition, that after lie had pained some time in great agonies, and horrors of mind, lie begged those who had the care of burying him to dress his body in the habit of a Capuchin, that the Devil might not run away with it, and to do further justice to himself, he desired them to tie an halter about
his neck as a mark of that ignominious punishment which in his own thoughts he had so justly deserved. Christianstcd, St. Croix, 22nd October, 1855. 1 1 EG ESI AS.

The demise of the Consort of Mr William McFarlane lias awakened the deepest sympathy in the breasts of all who know and honestly appreciate the worth of that much-respected and highly-esteemed gentleman. Of the deceased, it is enough only to name her to those who knew her; and the remembrance of her kind, courteous, and gentle disposition þÿ her affable manners and lady-like demeanor, must at once call forth those feelings of regret for her departure so natural to humanity. But she has gone where " the weary are at rest" þÿ to that world where the spirits of the just are made perfect, there to enjoy everlastingly the bliss of the redeemed. With this anticipated hope, we leave her, to offer our condolence to her bereaved husband, whose feelings have been so powerfully wrought upou by this visitation of Divine Providence. But we pray that that same Providence might give hiin strength of mind to bear this (to him) irreparable loss with christian fortitude ; and so establish his health, that he might long continue that usefulness which he has unweariedly struggled to maiutain. c. Most persons are fond of seeing the local newspaper þÿ and well they may ; but in our small community to be found a class of individuals is who are no supporters of the press, but abuse it, and yet these very parties are the first to catch the paper þÿ " hot from the press" þÿ and almost read holes in it. We are ever willing that any one who cannot really afford to subscribe to our journal, and is a well-wisher, may have a gratis perusal of it ; but wo look low upon the man whose coffers arc o'crflowing, and yet would stoop to borrow his neighbour's paper, knowing that he himself is in a far better pecuniary posision than the lender. We have read of a man who sent his son to a neighbour to borrow the newspaper for a few minutes as he only wanted to read it. The paper was delivered, and the lad requested to ask bis father for the loan of his dinner as ho (the loaner of the paper) only wanted to eat it ! We find a simile in this ; after a paper is read it becomes useless þÿ so with a meal, after it is eaten the appetite for it is lost. Wc hope that this hint in time may not offend the mass, but have the effect of teaching some a sense of their duty.

Ho takes a common lithographic stone, and pours on it a solution of bitumen in sulphuric ether. In a few i seconds the ether evaporates, leaving a | very delicate and thin contingof bitumen, the stone exhibiting a surface like a i plate prepared for etching. He then takes a negative obtained by the collodion or calotype process, and applies it to the stone, and then places it in the full light of the sun. Within a moderate time the negative communicates an impression to the bitumen very faintly visible. The negative is removed and the bitumen is placed in a bath of sulphuric ether which dissolves the whole of the bitumen not acted on by the light, and there remains a photographic picture represented accurately on the stone in the undissolved bitumen. The stone may then be placed in the hands of a lithographic printer and printed from."

The Russians in flic Northern Fort. From flic London Morning Chronicle. At last some information of a precise and not very agreeable nature lias arrived from the seat of war. The Emperor of Russia, alarmed by the danger to which that part of his dominions is exposed, lias set out in person for the Crimea, and at the latest date bad arrived at Odessa. That incident, however, is not so startling ; it speaks rather of alarm on the part of the enemy, and need not raise apprehensions in our mind. Rut it is not so pleasant to be told that the Russians find themselves in a condition to hold the Northern forts, which they are busied in strengthening, throwing up new works at every vulnerable point. The magnitude of the previous success bad somewhat dazzled our eyes in reference to these fortresses, and wc were willing to believe that the enemy would not long continue to hold them. Even now we incline to the opinion that they will not long oppose obstacles to the advance of the allied troops. They are now of comparatively little use to the enemy ; for they cover nothing þÿ they threaten nothing. They arc mere isolated posts which an enemy, bent on a desperate and blind resistance, might be expected tenaciously to defend ; but which present no points of strategic importance. ... The allied base of opera- . tion is independent of them, and the worst they can do is to prevent the harbour being used by our llects and merchantmen, which, in the coming winter, would be of advantage to our marine. But, more than all, it is as an indication

of the strength of the Russian army that the intelligence is most significant. It is plain that their resources in the Crimea are not yet exhausted, and that they have no intention of leaving it, or they would not now be fortifying themselves on the Southern extremity of the peninsula. We must, therefore, make up our minds to a renewal of the struggle on ground little removed from the

spot where it has already been fought so desperately. Be it so, France and England are prepared for the emergency. Supplies, in men and materiel , are finding their way in immense numbers to the country that has already absorbed so much, and still gapes for more. With armies amply equipped, abundantly supplied, high in hope, Hushed with recent victory, and panting for further success, we cannot doubt that this campaign will end as arduously, perhaps, but, at the same time, as gloriously, as. its continuance hitherto has proved.

This explains the promptitude with which those Powers sent their order to St. Domingo O to cancel the treaty with the United States, and which they effected without the least remonstrance from our Cabinet. RUMOURS OF NEGOTIATION The German papers ore full of rumours relating to an alleged proposal to renew

negotiations with Russia. The Frankfort Post Gazette is informed by a letter dated Vienna, Sept 14, that " a fresh attempt is to be nyrde to re-establish peace. A fresli note will be sent to Russia, through the medium of Austria. In this note the demands of the Allied Powers will be once more explicitly stated, and the proposition will be made for reopening negotiations on this basis. Should Russia not accept this proposition, the military convention between Austria and the Western Powers will be immediately ratified. Respecting the demands of the Western Powers, the assurance has been given that they are still moderate to an eminent degree. The original programme has been retained ; nor has a single point been added that is not lire natural consequence of the military advantages obtained. Among these consequences is an indemnity for war expenses, which will doubtless figure as the most important feature of the new negotiations. A fresh treaty is spoken of as having been concluded between France and England on the one pait, and Turkey on the other. Its object is to invest the Western Powers with the right ol keepiug garrisons in various parts of Turkey. The points specified are Varna, Adrianople, Constantinople, and Gallipoli. Varna and Sinope would be used as maritime stations by the Western Powers." The Corriere Italiano of Vienna, a paper often quoted as semi-official, says: þÿ "The course to be followed by the Allies in the Crimea after the taking of Sebastopol will

depend on the attitude of the States of Central Europe. A more energetic policy on the part of our Cabinet, we are firmly persuaded, is the only one capable of accelerating the conclusion of a peace so ardently desired by all Europe." " A more energetic policy" on the part of Austria will have very little weight with the Western Powers if tie energy is to be exercised on behalf of Russia.

The Burgher Council has in due time to draw up a yearly estimate of the probable expenses the municipality will have to defray in the following year, j which estimate shall comprise not only the expenses attending the general municipal administration, hut also the amounts required for those branches of the municipal economy, which are under a separate ad ministration. The estimate must besides contain an exposition of the means possessed to defray the expenses. If no particular circumstance makes it probable that the expences, or the revenues for defraying the same, will be more or less, than what has been amounts are to be entered in the new one. Regard- adopted in the estimate nearest preceding, the same j of the Superior ing the amounts required for the separate branches of the administration, viz. to the school-department &c., the respective commissions or officials have in due time, at the request of the Burgher Council, to forward to the same their calculations of what is required. If there should be found any cause to re-

duce the amount demanded, the matter is to be deliberated with the respective commissions or officials, and if an agreement is not attained, the case is to be submitted to the Superior Authority who will decide what is to be defrayed. The whole estimate is thereafter to be forwarded to the Superior Authority, who, provided it finds nothing to observe, will return the same with its approval. In the contrary case the Burgher Council will be informed of the remarks the Superior Authority has found it requisite to make, and if the Burgher Council after having taken the case in consideration, do not admit the correctness of said remarks, it is bound, within 14 days, to send in a written representation on the subject which will be submitted by the Government to the decision of the Ministry of Finance, and until such decision arrives the amounts in question are to be entered in the estimate as in the one for the preceding year. If during the year question arises of expenses beyond those entered in the estimate, the Burgher I not Council has to report the matter in the same manner as prescribed regarding the yearly estimate, and arc in general with regard to these expenses the same rules to be followed as stated above: however, in cases, where the decision of the Ministry of Finances has been demanded, but circumstances do not admit any delay, the order of the Government is meanwhile to be complied with. $ iy. It is incumbent on the Burgher Council to have a most exact control with the mouey-aifairs of the

municipality, consequently to attend to that the municipal Taxes as well as other revenues are correctly and in due time collected, and, if necessary to propose that their payment be enforced, likewise that the amount is appropriated to defray the municipal expenses, and until required be safely deposited in the manner as approved by the Superior Authority according to the proposal of the Burgher Council at each place. An exact account shall be kept of the municipal revenues and expenditure and in particular a cash-book in which every item of revenue and expenditure is to be entered on the day they take place. The cash-book is to be closed every month, so as to show the balance the land treasury has on hand at that time. In St. Croix and St. Thomas there shall also be kept a ledger. The Burgher Council shall attend to, that works undertaken at the expense of the land treasury, are executed in the best and most economical manner. $ 20. Burgher Council, unless circumstances demand that such a measure be executed without delay ; in the same manner the sanction Authority must be obtained previous to any disbursement being made from the land-trea-

sury. Communication. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Meteorological. St. Croix, 17th Octr., 1855. Sir þÿ lu vour u St. Croix Avis" of 9th inst., you have introduced some useful Meteorological observations regarding the Barometer, Hurri- canes (now called Cyclones), leave to offer a few remarks, the result and ol 1 many take years attentive application to the same subjects at this Island, and first of the Barometer. The proper height of the quicksilver in the Barometer at the level ol the sea can be considered as 30 inches English. In common weather, there are in the 24 hours 4 regular oscillations in its height, varying in these latitudes from 6-10ths to 8-10ths of a line, as follows : At 10 o'clock in the forenoon the quicksilver is at its highest state ; at 4 o'clock in the afternoon it is at its lowest, being from 6-lOths to 8-10ths of a line lower than at 10 o'clock in the torenoon ; by 10 o'clock at night it will have regained its former height of 10 in the forenoon, and by 1 o'clock in the morning, it will have descended to its lowest state, to return by 10 o'clock in the forenoon to its highest state for that day, and this with constant regularity (Hurricanes, Pamperos, excepted.) This has loug been noticed, but its cause I bequently attempted" lieve remains as yet a mystery. I have fre- to find "some clue to unfold the cause, but all to no purpose. The Sun, I conceive, is the principal agent. During the year (excepting in the hurricane season i, that highest state will rarely deviate one line front its mean state, and in the hurri-

cane season, if it should even deviate two lines lower, but the oscillations regularly going on, in I feel no alarm ; but, if after 4 o'clock, either the morning or afternoon, the mercury in place of rising continues to fall, there is then every reason for suspicion. The absolute height of the mercury in these latitudes is of IMPORTANCE. I have never noiieed the mercury to stand three lines below its standard, without its being followed by or accompanied with a Cyclone, or Pampero with a deluge. 2. The remarks ou the Barometer in this paragraph are excellent. 4 In this I entirely agree, but will extend this further in $ 4. t. The common direction of progression of a Hurricane in these latitudes, say from Barbados to Porto Rico, may be considered from E N E to \V V W true (the variation of the compass is small at St. Croix 1£ E.) VV., at which it will continuo till the meteor passes. We will now suppose the Storm to begin at N N.W. Lord Pnlmersitoii oil (he War. The following outlines of a reply from Lord Palmerston to an address presented to him at Broadlands (the Premier's seat) may be read with interest. The noble Viscount said : þÿ " The oapture of Sebastopol is an event of which every Englishman may be proud. It is an event of which our Allies þÿ the French, the Sardinians, and the Turks þÿ may also be proud. In is an event which must inspire joy and exultation in the breast of every generous free man on the surface of the globe. We have been told, by the commander of the Russian army, that in evacuating the town of SebaBtopol, he left nothing to the allies but ' blood-stained ruins and, no doubt, as far as depended upon him þÿ as far as time allowed þÿ as far as his means of destruction extended, it was his intention to leave nothing elso to the victorious enemy. But, although in retiring, he blew up fortified works þÿ although he exploded great magazines of powder þÿ although he destroyed everything that could be burned within the time allowed for his remaining stay, yet we know that, when the allies entered the town, they found among its blood-stained ruins no less than 4,000 pieces of cannon, an immense quantity of powder, an enormous amount of can non balls and shells, and materials of various kinds, necessary for the prosecution of war What does that teach us on reflection ? Why, does it not show the vast importance which the Government of Russia attached to that strong hold of Russian power in the Black Sea Why was that vast accumulation of warlike material

made, more than could have been required for the most prolonged defence of the place ? Why was it that, elements were there accumulated for supplying great armies aud for furnishing gn at fleets ? Why, it was because they felt that In Sebastopol was the stronghold of their power in the East þÿ that from that centre was to radiate that intense and extensive power which was to lead them to the conquest of Constantinople, and to lead them -from that centre of empire to sway the destinies of Europe. Well, then, that I think affords a satisfactory proof of the sound judgment which was exercised by the allied Governments in directing against Sebastopol the great power of their army and navy in the Black Sea Wo have heard much of the sicgo of Sebastopol, and of the gallant defence of the garrison which held that town ; and yet I may be permitted to say that, in the proper sense of the word, there has been no siege at all. and that Sebastopol has not been defended by any garrison Why, a garrison means a comparatively small military force, which, shut up witbiu the walls of a town or fortress, defends itself against a vastly superior army. A siege means an operation which is conducted by a superior force investing such a fortress, cutting off its communication with the rear, and, by approaches which are familiar to military men, at last make a breach in the defences, and then, by bringing au-

l>eiior numbers against the interior amount of the garrison, overwhelming them, as must he the case in so unequal a struggle But that which has happened in the Crimea has been a transaction of a totally ditferent kind The allied armies of England and France, assisted from the beginning by a portion of the T urkish forces ; assisted materially by the brave Sardinians þÿ a body of troops worthy of admiration by all, for their discipline, their skill, their science, their good order, and their bravery þÿ that allied army has for 12 months I was going to say 12 long months, and long I must call them, although 12 months be a short period of historical time, yet it has been pregnant with so many vast events, that it must be long in occupying its page in the history of Europe þÿ that, allied army has during that period not been besieging a single town, or attacking a single garrison, but it has been fighting the entire military forces of the Russian Empire. We have been contending not merely with an army in the Crimea, equal and sometimes superior to our own numbers, but 1 say it without exaggeration, we have been contending with the entre military resources of that vast military empire þÿ an empire which devotes a great part of its revenues to the maintenance of an enormous standing army þÿ an army which thoy call a million of men, but which may be set down at S00,000 men. War is, no doubt, a calamity ; but the course of the present war has brought its evils as little home to the

To the General-in-Chief þÿ Sir, I have thought that at the moment when Sebastopol lias just fallen beneath the blows of the Allied armies, it was my duty to signalise to my Gcvernment the excellent services which the English officers attached to my staff, as Commissioners of Her Majesty the Queen, have given without intermission. The letter, of which I append a copy, will enable you to appreciate the terms in which I have thought it my duty to make this communication, which I hope will attain the end I propose, more especially if you will join your efforts to mine in obtaining for those two officers the rewards of which they are in every way worthy. Accept, &.C., (Signed) Le Marechal A. PELISSIER. To His Excellency the General-in- Chief of the English Army.

Head Quarters, Sept. 12, 1855. M. la þÿMarechal, I have already had occasion, as well as my predecessors, to call on your kind intervention to press upon the British Government the incessant and most valuable services which, from the commencement of this war, Major-General Hugh Rose and Lieutenant-Colonel St. George Foley, the Commissioners of Her Majesty the Queen at the French head quarters, have continually rendered. On the 7th and J8th of June, on the 16th of August, and especially on the 8th of September, these two officers seemed ubiquitous in maintaining verbal and constant communications between the two armies; and to effect this they frequently fulfilled the most dangerous missions. It would be utterly superfluous for me to state here how they acquitted them selves of their military duties. The capture of Sebastopol is too happy an event to render it necessary for me to renew my request, that you will cause the English Government to be made aware of the expression of my regard towards these two officers, and of my desire to see them both obtain those rewards which they have so worthily deserved. I shall be very happy, M. le Marechal, if you will promptly forward this renewed application on my part, in the manner you may think most conducive to the interests of these two officers. Accept &c., (Signed) Le Marechal A. PELISSIER His Excellency the Minister of War.
Kiteimive Robbery of IT. S Govern men t Money. FIFTY THOUSAND DOLLARS STOLEN

On Friday morning last an extensive robbery of government money was discovered in the office of the American Express Company, No. 62 Broadway. The circumstances of the case are as follows : þÿ It appears that this company arc constantly receiving from the vari-

ous government land offices out West sums of money of different amounts, which, on their arrival in this city are immediately delivered at the United States Sub-Treasury. Two boxes, which it was believed contained coin to the amount of $ 25,000 in each, were received 011 Friday morning from Dubuque, Iowa, directed to the Sub-Treasury. They were in apparent good order, sealed and iron bound, but as one of the lids was a little loose, it attracted the attention of the receiving clerk. On shaking the box, bis suspicions were immediately aroused. Instead of the light jingle of gold, its contents had the dull, heavy, sound oflead. Before opening the box, however, he informed the President, Mr. Henry Wells, who directed it to lie delivered immediately at the Sub-Treasury, and who went there himself to witness its examination. Several of the officers were called in, and in their presence the seal was broken and the lid raised, when, instead of 8 25,000 in gold coin, it was found to contain 175 pounds of rifle bullets, and 26 pounds of sheet lead. The other box was opened, and the same amount of lead discovered in it. The Chief of Police was immediately sent for, and the matter placed in his hands. No clue could be obtained as to where the robbery was committed ; but from the extensive arrangements which have been made by the Chief, the perpetrators cannot long elude detection. Two police officers were despatched to Dubuque, and others were also sent from Buffalo to the same place, while the
police of the principal towns and villages for several hundred miles around have been informed of the particulars. þÿ N. Y. Herald.

What the Steam Engine does. This afternoon we received to our address from West End an article intended, no doubt, for insertion, enumerating seventy acts which the Steam Engine is capable of performing. Pity it does not also pre-pay postage, for then we should not have occasion to complain so repeatedly. We must theu positively refuse insertion to the article in question, since our liberal correspondent has not acted up to the rules laid down by us, and published in every number of the Avis, namely, " The postage on letters to this Office from West End or St. Thomas must be prepaid, or no notice will be taken of the same."

The "Industry" again! We have good authority for stating that the Packet from Southampton was seen steaming into St. Thomas on Thursday morning, and yet it was not till this afternoon that the letters and newspapers were received here. A fault lies somewhere ; we cannot say, but leave the public to determine where. This much wc arc certain of that the substitute packet was telegraphed to be in sight at an early hour this morning ; and had it not been for the exertions of some of our merchants, who sent off a row-boat to the sloop, wo should have been up to the present time of our writing þÿ 4 p. m. þÿ without an item of intelligence ; had this boat, however, been led by fishermen the turtle passage," instead dispatched to the sloop through the channel cal- " of the ships' channel, much delay would have been avoided þÿ and the mails landed in one hall the time. Whilst treating on this subject, we cannot but wonder at the apparent nonchalance of our Postmaster in serving the reading public , for altho' the mails þÿ a small hag þÿ were landed at 2 p. ra , it was not before eight or ten minutes

of 3 o'clock that the newspapers could be arrived at. Surely, with such laborious work, some assistants are required ! Let the news be what it may, we should have it in season. Moon's Eclipse. þÿ This interesting given phenomenon, due of notice the readers The Chronicle of which was last week, passed in all its grandeur before the observation of many who kept awake to view it on Thursday morning. The commencement of it was not very per ceptible owing to a gathering of heavyclouds at the time, hut at 20 minutes past 2, which was 18 minutes before the commencement of the total eclipse, the phenomenon was revealed in perfection, and we do not remember having ever witnessed an eclipse under more favourable circumstances. In our next publication the notes of our scientific old friend Piiilologus will he given to enlighten our readers more fully on the subject þÿ Chronicle, October 27.

FIC EE-MASONIC V. The principles of Free Masonry are two in number, and but two. These are þÿ piety touarils God, and brotherly love. There are no other legitimate and radical principles in the constitution of Free Masonry. There are indeed some appropriate regulations ; but of these relate solely to the preservation good order and decorous behaviour among the brethren towards each other at their meetings. And it is a rule of t he institution that there should be neither cursing nor swearing, nor uncharitable contentions, nor angry disputations, while they remain together in the Lodge ; and that no subjects relating to the Constitution, either in Church or State, shall be introduced at Masonic meetings. Free Masonry disclaims and abhors irreligion and treasonable principles We cannot prevent Masonry from being called mere mummery by those who choose to do so ; but I contend that it is not only founded on the best principles of the human heart, whereby it has been more permanent, and less changed in its form, than any other mere institution, notwithstanding the long period of its duration, but it lias also done much good. Its charitable funds are open to the relief of strangers, as well as of Masonic brethren when reduced The knowledge of Free to every traveller introducing him to Masonry is a letter þÿ of recommendation the company and acquaintance of some of the best and most respected citizens of every nation in the world ; and by which many have made a fortune more easily, and more largely than they would

have done without this advantage. As Free Masonry is universal, it might be made subservient to the purpose of propogating the Christian religion among the Heathen, by initiating them into the gospel views of piety and charity. Though it be objected to Masonry, that the form of its regulations is kept a secret from all except initiated brethren, yet I answer, that Free Masons do not refuse to make any one acquainted with the secrets of their institution who wish to join their society, and who are men of good character. And 1 would ask

a A T 4X where can a man spend an evening with more of the exercise of a friendly heart, and at less expense, than in a Lodge of Free Masons The best things may, no doubt, be abused, but attendance in the Lodges of Free Masons afford no direct temptation to be intemperate in anything. Neither have Masonic meetings any tendency to corrupt men's morals, nor to hurt the peace in Church or State. þÿ From a Sermon by a Rev. Dr. and Brother.

Christiansted, St. Croix. TUESDAY , 6 th NOVEMBER , 1855. Arrival ol' llic Governor.
IDs Excellency Governor Schlegel and Lady returned here on Saturday from a tour to the Sister Islands, and landed under a salute of 15 guns from the Fort.

3 1 A 2 3« Her Britannic Majesty's surveying-schooner harbour in gallant style yesterday afternoon, Scorpion, Commander Parsons, entered and our while under sail fired a salute of 17 guns in compliment to His Excellency the Governor, which was immediately replied to by the Fort. The Daily News says : þÿ " We believe that there is no doubt of the faot that General Simpson has resigned his command in the Crimea, and has recommended General Eyre as his successor. The Government however, have declined to accept General Simpson's resignation. A BRITISH FLEET SENT TO THE COAST OF ITALY. Her Majesty's ships Rodney, Albion, London, Leander, and Wasp, have received orders to proceed, under the command of Admiral Stopford, to the coast of Italy.
