The Annual Examination. The Annual Public Examination of the Scholars attending the Danish and Lancasterian Schools took place on Tuesday last, the lith iust., in presence of Ilis Excellency the Governor and Lady, and a large number of respectable Inhabitants. The examinations were proceeded with as usual, and seemed to give executed general satisfaction. the female The elegant needlework, admiration by scholars, excited the ol all ; and reflects great honor on the teachers in this department. The Lancasterian School was well attended, and progresses very favorably. This school will, no doubt, prove highly beneficial to the community in the future. What seems mostly to strike a visitor ofthc Danish School is the anomaly of teaching Geography and History in the Danish language, which is scarcely comprehensible to the scholars. This language, in our opinion, ought to ho taught separately, as any other language from The system pursued is objectionable attainment of would be. its presenting obstacles to the speedy have these branches ; since, not only the children to overcome tlio difficulties which these studies present, hut they have, at the same time, to struggle with the intricacies of a language which, not being properly understood by them, affords a very imperfect vehicle for the conveyance of knowledge. The result of this practice is, as must, ho expected, a mere lip -acquirement of

whole chapters in the works used, without that understanding of the lesson necessary for its retention. The lessons, we know, arc translated into English by the teacher ; hut this does not assist the memory of the child, since what has been learnt by rote is that which will he remembered, and which, in this case, consist of mere sentences, unintelligible to the scholar without the aid of a teacher. AVe make these remarks, not in the spirit of fault-finding, hut simply as a statement of things as they appear to us, and recommend our observations to the consideration of those who are competent to decide this question. The present occasion affords a fit opportunity for a few remarks on the contemplated extension of the School. As far as we understand, this extension relates to the lower or Lancasterian school, where all our children, not now receiving instruction, are to be taught reading and writing This is an extension to the Colonies of the fine system pursued in Denmark, where the State compels the attendance of every child at the common schools. From the declining prosperity of these Islands, the ability of parents in general to have their children educated in Europe or America, is very limited ; and, consequently, comparatively few children are sent away for that purpose. This state of things seems to call for the establishment of a department for higher instruction than that now obtainable. Such an Institution, under existing circumstances, cannot fail of being sup-

ported. Let it he open to the scholars, not only of the Danish and Lancasterian schools, but also of the privato schools in these Islands, provided they can stand an examination in those branches, þÿ the knowledge of which may be made the basis of admission. Thus would he exerted an influence which would reach down through all the private and primary schools, and affect the entire system ot instruction. The pupils of all our schools, with their teachers, will have a stimulus and a prize which will awaken both interest and ambition.

FRANCE. From the London Weekly Dispatch. The Paris correspondent of the Daily News writes : þÿ A Council of Ministers, at which the Emperor presided, was held on Wednesday morning at St. Cloud, and sat several hours. Notwithstanding the repeated assertions of the German newspapers that M. þÿProkesch-Osten s visit to Paris was merely private, 1 believe it to be certain that the main subject of the deliberations of the Council was a proposition for peace, suggested by Austria, and which she undertakes to say that Russia would accept. It is rumoured that France and England would not insist upon retaining the Crimea, but that they do make the payment of the expenses of the war a sine </un non. This, we may be very sure, is no part of the Austrian proposal I think it not rash to conjecture, that the result of the deliberations of this þÿday Council s has been hostile to the certainly inglorious terms of peace which Austria would fain persuade the allies to consent to, although there is doubtless a Peace party in the French Cabinet. Indeed the unusually protracted discussion (for the Council, which met at 10 þÿo clock, did not separate till 2) infers a considerable difference of opinion. I have myself little doubt that an articlo in this þÿday s Constitutionnel by the favourite Government writer, M. Granier dc Cassagnac, contains by anticipation the Imperial decision which the Ministerial Council was in point of fact merely called upon to register. M de Cassagnac, treating of the course which the

allies arc likely to pursue, throws it in the teeth of Russia that her diplomatists, not long since, insisted that fails accomplis must be taken as starting points of negotiations. þÿ The fleet of Sebastopol still þÿexists, said she, þÿ reduce it by force if you can, but you cannot oblige us to destroy it with our own þÿhands. þÿ Now þÿwhat, he continues, þÿ are these faits accomplis ? They arc, not the reduction, but the destruction, of the Russian fleet, the destruction of Sebastopol, the uncontested possession of the Black Sea and the Sea of AzofF, with the certain and speedy capture of all the Crimea looming in the horizon. These are, therefore, the bases upon which any new conferences, whether they be held at Vienna or elsewhere, must þÿrest. Nothing but the conquest of the whole Crimea, the writer implies, will satisfy the Western Powers as a guarantee against the ambition of þÿRussia. The opinion at Paris becomes more and more confirmed that the Russians will not only abandon the Northern forts, but that their whole army is now making a decided movement of retreat. As the intention of the allied forces appears to be to threaten the right of the Russian army from Eupatoria, and the left by Beider, by taking it in the rear, it becomes very difficult for the Russians to maintain themselves in the positions they occupy on the plateau of the Tchernaya. It cannot, therefore, be astonishing that Prince Gortschakoff, finding it impossible to defend himself, should decide on retreating.

From the New York papers we learn that some excitement prevailed in that City, occasioned by the arrest of several members of the þÿ Free Love þÿAssociation for offensive speeches. 1 bis Association appears to be of a dangerous character, with very dubious claims to the possession of moral principle. Its doctrinos of þÿ Individual þÿSovereignty and þÿ Passional þÿAttraction appear to be totally subversive of all social order ; and perhaps, if allowed to go on unchecked, even of decency. They repudiate the present system of marriage, deny the right of society or the State to interfere in any way with the subject, further than it may rightfully interfere with any civil contract ; and contend that marriage may be a limited or life partnership, at the option of the man and woman, who are the sole and rightful judges of the time and manner of its beginning and termination.

From Thursday evening till Friday morning we had a continuous fall of water, with repeated flashes of lightning and rapid peals of near and distant thunder On Saturday afternoon the rain re-commenced, with mild and pleasant weather, until Sunday morning. Bare-faced Robbery. þÿ We learn that this morning a black man (unknown) deliberately entered a shop (kept by Miss Jane Fletcher) in þÿCompany street, s helped himself to some pieces of merchandize, and took to his heels towards the country. It appears that the shop had a blind or jalousie door, which being closed, the parties retired to another part of the house ; the man was seen from up stairs to enter the shop, but supposing him to be a purchaser, and believing that there were persons in the establishment, no alarm whatever was given by the individual who saw him. The perpetration of such a bold broad-day piece of vilhany we seldom hear of We are also told that there are several night marauders who, grovelling in the dark like demons, go about to þÿ þÿhave-a-care, lest they be unexpectedly stoning houses. The Monittur of Sunday contained the follow ing official paragraph : þÿ þÿ The Government of the Emperor have seen with profound regret the publication of a letter on the affairs of Naples, and which would lead to the supposition that the policy of the Emperor, instead of being frank and loyal as it has ever been with respect to foreign Governments, would favour, in an underhand manner, certain pretensions. The Govern ment disavow them in the most formal manner, and under whatsoever form they may be preþÿsented. In reference to this paragraph, the Paris correspondent of the Times says : þÿ þÿ The few remarks I ventured to remark have not been entirely useless, ft was time for the Emperor to intervene as the pretensions of Prince Murat, un founded and absurd as they are, and I sincerely believe quite against the wishes of his Majesty, wero beginning to produce an unpleasant effect among public men, who, whatever be their estimate of the present King of Naples, do not, of a surety deem Prince Murat to be exactly the man for his successor, even in the event of the patience of his people becoming exhausted. The highest station is not exempt from care. The pretensions and quarrels of the brothers and sisters of the first Napoleon formed no small part of his annoyances ; and if the truth were known the third of the name can boast of no immunity in that respect. An altercation is rumoured

to have occurred very recently between the Emperor and one of the family þÿ perhaps, Prince Murat himself. You have nothing of your þÿuncle, was the reproach, addressed with bitter emphasis, to his Majesty. þÿ Alas ! 1 have his þÿfamily, was the reply, made with sarcastic þÿresignation. The same correspondent adds : þÿ þÿ Among the rumours which are circulated þÿ rather mysteriously, it is true, in two or three political circles þÿ is one which 1 have refrained from noticing hith&rto. Its revival in a more general, if not a more consistent, form than before makes me now allude to it. This rumour refers to an alleged matrimonial alliance between Prince Napoleon and a Princess of the Royal family of England. Whether there be any foundation for it I am unable to say, and only relate it as it is reported. The friends of the Imperial dynasty reason, it appears, i.i this manner : þÿ þÿ Theold prejudices which separated France and England have disappeared, like the smoke from the field of battle. The glory won in common, the dangers shared by brothers in arms, the sentiments of esteem and affection cemented by the generous blood which both have shed in combating the same enemy, the resistance they have shown together for two years not only to Russia, in arms against them, but to the intrigues of Germany, which looks on and þÿwaits all concur in uniting and linking each day stronger and closer the two greatest nations of the earth, and it would be rather with France that England should seek a matrimonial

alliance than with Prussia, whose sympathies and whose wishes are well known to be for Russia, and Russia þÿalone. They add, that Prince Napoleon is also of Royal race, and is even connected with the Royal family of England by his mother, the Princess Catherine of Wurtemburg, who herself was a daughter of a Princess of Brunswick. But, independently of that relationship, they look upon an alliance of this kind as a combination far more suitable, more useful, more politic than the other, and one which would be more in conformity with live actual relations of the two þÿcountries.

America. The Great News. þÿ The news of the fall of Sebastopol created the greatest excitement that the city has experienced since the loss of the Arctic. We pnblished the first despatches at half-past 2 on Thursday afternoon, and between that time and 8 þÿo clock on Friday morning 80,000 sheets of the Herald were printed and distributed all over the country. The celerity with which the news was received and printed is quite as wonderful as the siege itself. The event took place on the 9th of September, and by the aid of the telegraph and our fast ocean steamships we are able to give an extended account of it in less than 20 days afterwards. This must slightly astonish our elderly citizens, who were obliged to wait three months for very meagre and one-sided reports of the battles of the first Napoleon. Things are changed now. The age of steam and electricity have brought about many wonders in war, diplomacy, and newspapers. The effect of the news on our English and French residents was almost overpowering. Subjected as they have been for the past eight or nine months to the sarcasms of the pro-Russian party, they had become almost disheartened. The little bits of glory, from time to time, did not approximate their boasts when the war commenced, and they could not retort upon their opponents. But on Thursday night, when there was no doubt that a part of the Gibraltar of the Black Sea had fallen, they had good cause to rejoice, and they improve the occasion to the fullest extent. þÿ New York

Lobster-pond at Hamble, in the Southampton Water. þÿ The pond, or stew, is artificial, about fifty yards square, by ten or twelve feet deep, with shelving sides of brick or stone, and cement, with concrete bottom, having a lock, or weir, at the entrance for the admission or exit of salt-water at the bottom (the Hamble being a fresh-water stream). This pond cost about £1,300. The lobsters arc fed on fish and fatten. A recent visit to the establishment, in August, 1854, there were 70,000 in prime condition, although the summer had been very hot All weak lobsters aro kept in baskets and sold first. These lobsters are brought from the coast of Brittany and Ireland, in sailing welled smacks, about 60 tons, which carry 7,000 to 9,000 each Lobster carrying is subject to tho following contingencies ; thunder kills them when in the well, also proximity to the discharge of heavy ordnance. Communication. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Mr. Editor, þÿ Amusements of any kind aro so rare in our little Island that 1 cannot but express, through the medium of your columns, tho great satisfaction which I, and I may venture to say all, enjoyed who witnessed the St. Croix Races on Saturday last. Strange to say that the bustle, confusion, accidents, and betting disputes which usually occur on suob days, were not to be seen ; to the contrary, tho greatest order and decorum prevailed, and amoDg a great number of persons of all classes who had assembled there, 1 believe that with the exception of a cart being upturned in the the gut, first the riders in and a slight fall of one of race from a refractory horse, no other damage happened for the day. It is, therefore, to be hoped that these Races may be continued yearly or half-yearly ; I havo at least heard so, and that the next will come off in April þÿ 56, þÿ if so, we look forward with anxiety to the period. Before concluding, I cannot but admire the calmness and proper direction of F. R. Newton, Esq., to whom indeed we are indebted for the whole affair. Yours, T. M. Christiansted, December 12.

Hajor Wolff. Few voyagers, whoso lot it was to pass through St. þÿThomas s, will have failed to notice our muchrespected co-religionist, Major Wolff, manager of the bank there, and commander of the insular national guard. Active for the public weal and always ready, in the spirit of a true Israelite, to serve his fellow men, irrespective of race or creed, this gentleman, being on leave of absence in Europe, lias just returned to London from a trip to the capital of Denmark, to which king dom, as known, the island belongs. The major, we learn, met, as he deserves, with a very gratifying reception at Copenhagen. At the drawingroom held by his majesty on bis birth-day, the Gth ult , the welcome visitor was presented to the king by special command ; and on the Monday following, be had the honour of being most graciously received by his sovereign in a special audience. The monarch conversed with him some time on the state of the Jewish community, expressing his surprise when he heard that it had only- a reader, and was at present without a minister, and without confirmation of youth, a state of things which the king considered incorrect. At an interview which the major had with the bishop that gentleman called the attention of the prelate to the state of the coloured Lutheran population of the island, which had some time ago applied for permission to use an American ritual preferred by them to that authorised. Warmly representing that delay might estrange the petitioners from their present communion, the bishop

naturally asked, þÿ Arc you a Lutheran þÿr þÿ No, replied the advocate of the coloured population, þÿ I have the honour to be an Israelite : and as such 1 deem it my duty to espouse warmly the cause of civil and religious liberty in general, and especially of those whose request appears to me

þÿjust. The prelate was so pleased with the zeal aud straightforwardness of the honest Jew, that he invited him to pay him another visit, and brought the subject immediately under the notice of the colonial minister, with every prospect of meeting with a speedy and satisfactory solution. þÿ London Jewish Chronicle.

The preparations of our government for the new state of things at San Juan del Norte are somewhat active, in a diplomatic and naval regard. Despatches of some moment have been forwarded to our Minister in Nicaragua, Mr. Wheeler. Though iutimations have been thrown out that he is himself complicated with our fillibusteros, it is not probable that he will neglect to obey orders. The fact is one which now requires not only skill but energy. Com. Paulding was brought here by a despatch from the government, and has left with his instructions, to proceed to San Juan, with the force fitted out for his command, at the Brooklyn Navy Yard. He will probably meet, at the tristing place, a large British naval force, under the command of Admiral Fanshaw. It once happened, on the occasion of the Prometheus difficulty, that one of our vessels of war was sent to the same place, and there met a vastly superior naval force ; but instead of inviting a combat, a la Hollins , our officers accepted and returned British hospitality with frequent and mutual entertainments, thus coming to a good understanding. It is not so good a feeling that prevails at this time. It is believed here that a British expeditionary

maica, and that the British flag will be hoisted at Punta Arenas, at Fort San Carlos up the river San Juan, and at Greytown. If the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty is no longer binding upon either party, this will certainly be the case ; and I know that this event is here looked to as one of probable occurrence. The U. S. Government put a certain interpretation upon the Treaty, requiring Great Britain to abandon her pretensions to the Bay Islands, and to relinquish, practically and absolutely, her Mosquito Protectorate. This was positively demanded and positively refused. If the British Government consider that the treaty is at an end, merely because they do not assent to our interpretation of it, it will be from a disposition to provoke a quarrel, which they can do, by taking military possession and establishing civil jurisdiction in Greytown. It is for our government, þÿ in case the British Government offers no such provocation as the above movement would imply, þÿ to offer to renew the negotiation from a new starting point. The moans of adjusting the question arc not exhausted, and can be readily found in a proper understanding with the government of Nicaragua, if any such government there bn.

You may rest assured that while the administration deem it politic to keep the public mind quiet, the most serious apprehensions are felt in regard to our present relation with England. We are on the very brink of a war. This question does not seem to be of difficult solution to any one who reflects that trade is opening new channels of incalculable extent across the American isthmus, and that the conthis highway is of equal importance to England the United States. Our people would be satisfied with the perfect neutrality of the isthmus routes, and their entire freedom to the general trade of the world. Hence our ready acquiescence in the Clayton-Bulwer treaty. In that convention the two Powers mutually guaranteed to protect construction and transit, and to maintain the neutrality and independence of all the isthmus communications from Tehuantepec to Darien ; but this plan was too moderate to suit British ideas of commercial empire. While the Clayton Bulwer treaty was still in force þÿ since neither party have proposed its abrogation þÿ England seized and colonized the Ruatan islands, equally in defiance of its obligations and ; of the sovereign rights of the State of Honduras, of whose territory she then took and still holds forcible and unjust possession. Advice to Consumptive Persons. þÿ Giving advice to consumptives Dr. Hall says : þÿ þÿ Eat all you can digest, and exercise a great deal in the open air, to convert what you eat into pure healthful blood. Do not be afraid of out-door air, day or night. Do not be afraid of sudden changes of weather ; let no change, hot or cold, keep you in doors. If it is rainy weather the more need of your going out, because you eat as much on a rainy day as a clear day, and if you exercise less, that much more remains in the system that ought to be thrown off by exercise, and some ill result, some consequent symptom or ill-feeling is the certaiu issue. If it is cold out of doors do not muffle your nose, eyes and mouth, in furs, veils, woollen comforters and the like ; nature has supplied you with the best muffler, with the best inhailing regulator, that is, two lips, shut them before you step out of a warm room into the cold air, and keep them shut until you have walked briskly a few rods and quickened the circulation a little ; walk fast enough to keep off a feeling

Look at a railway conductor going out of hot air iuto the piercing cold of winter, and in again, every five or ten minutes, and yet they do not take cold oftener than others ; you will scarcely find a consumptive man in a thousand of them. Communication. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Mr. Editor, þÿ Can you inform me how the following gross inconsistency which occurred a few days ago in West End, in connexion with the quarantine regulations can be explained : On the morning of the 1 1th instant the sloops Eliza and Francis Ann, having arrived from St. Thomas during the previous night, were quarantined twenty-four hours in consequence of having brought each a passenger ; they rode out their quarantine On the morning of the 12th the schooner Vigilant also arrived from St. Thomas, landed eighteen soldiers with their baggage, and three passengers, without any quarantine having been enforced. Why this difference should be "made between regular trading vessels and one partially employed by. the Government, and between civilians and soldiers, I cannot understand, unless disease and infection cannot be conveyed in the clothes of a soldier as readily as in those of the civilian. A St. Croix, December 13th, 1855.

f fles?" This apparent inconsistency may be explained on a consideration of the object for which a quarantine of 24 hours is enforced on vessels arriving from St. Thomas ; the object being to prevent an influx of passengers from that port, where they arc frequently transferred from vessels arriving from abroad to our packets, without even having landed. That disease and infection can or may be conveyed in the elothiDg of the military, as well as the civilian, is truo enough ; but then that personal knowledge of the non-existence of disease among a garrison is wanting in the case of a civiliau, and, of course, we need not suppose that Government would order a detachment of men into garrison here if Small Pox or any other dangerous disease existed among them while in St. Thomas. þÿ Editor.

We have been favored by a gentleman of this town with the loan of the New York Herald, of the 6th instant, from which the following extract is made : þÿ " BAD NEWS FROM þÿKANSAS CIVIL WAR AT þÿLAST UNITED STATES TROOPS ORDERED TO ASSIST THE EXECUTIVE. "We give this morning some very had news from Kansas Territory. The exciting questions which have made that Territory have at last brought about a civil war, and the abolitionist factions have taken up arms against the constituted authorities, appointed under the act id' Congress which erected a Territorial government. " The story, as we receive it through the St. Louis papers, and the despatches of our correspondent at that point, is as follows : " It sceuis that a man named Colcinan, who lives in a part of the Territory chiefly inhabited by members of the free State party, was ordered off his claim by three abolitionists. He resisted ; the assaulters were armed ; Colcmau shot one of them, and then gave himself up for trial. His house was then burned, and his wife and children driven out of the Territory. The Sheriff of the county was resisted in his endeavors to arrest the guilty parties þÿ the free State rose in open rebellion and defied the law. They were armed with rifles and had live pieces of cannon. The Sheriff's posse was in danger, and the Governor of the Territory was called upon. He issued a proclamation calling on tho people to assist the Sheriff in the execution of his duty. The posse was unable to take the assaulters of Coleman,

and the Governor called on the President of the United States for aid. The Washington papers of yesterday say that the President has ordered the United States troops at Fort Leavenworth to the assistance of Governor Shannon. Many persons had been frightened out of the Territory. Companies of outlaws were being drilled daily on the prairies. 14 This is what we make out of the accounts from Kansas which wc received yesterday. A civil war has commcncsd. Blood has already

been shed and the laws defied. It seems to us that the struggle will be protracted and bloody. With a weak President, without troops, with a Congress rent into so many factions that the initiative step to organization cannot be taken, with a civil war on the frontier, with a disturbed state of foreign relations þÿ with enemies without and traitors within þÿ we should think that Mr. Seward and his organs would be satisfied with the mischief they have already done. But, no : this Kansas war gives them abolition capital þÿ it will be the great question of the coming Presidential eauvass, swallowing up all minor matters, and if they will not realize the fate of the " engineer they will work it as long as possible. Let us see hoist with his own petard."

We have received the following telegraphic despatch from our Paris correspondent : þÿ PARIS, Monday, Nov. 19, 8 30 a.m. The Monileur announces that the Minister of War received yesterday the following telegraphic despatch from Marshal Pe'.issier, dated Sebastopol, Nov. 10, 6 p.m. Our park of artillery (called Park of the Mill) near lnkerman was partly destroyed yesterday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon by the explosion of three magazines containing altogether 30,000 kilogrammes of powder, 600,000 cartridges, 300 charged shells, aud other projectiles. The ignited materials, hurled to a distance, caused a violent conflagration in the English park next to ours, and there also partial explosions took place. At 6 o'clock the English and French workmen were masters of the fire. Our loss consist of' 30 killed, including two officers, and some hundred wounded, among whom are 10 officers. However sad such an event is, we must still congratulate ourselves that the consequences have not been more serious and disastrous I am not able to state the losses of our allies. I believe they are about the same as our own. As nearly always happens in similar cases, it is difficult to ascertain the cause of the first sion. explo- This is certainly a very lamentable accident ; but our stores are so considerable that the resources of the army arc not in the slightest degree affected by it.

According to accounts from the Crimea, says a letter from Vienna, of the 25th ultimo, a considerable portion of the cavalry which was embarked on the 15th November at Eupatoria and Kamiesch has been conveyed to Kertch. \ Good Wife. The good wife ! IIow much of this world's happiness and prosperity, says Mr. Burnap, is contained in the compass of these two short words ! Her influouce is immense. The power of a wife, for good or for evil, is altogether irresistible. Home must be the seat of happiness, or it must be for ever unknown. A good wife is to a man wisdom, and courage, and strength, and hope and endurance ; a bad one is confusion, weakness, discomfiture, despair. No condition is hopeless when the wife possesses firmness, decision, energy, economy. There is no outward prosperity which can counteract indolence, folly, and extravagance at home. No spirit can long resist bad domestic influences. Man is strong, but his heart is not adamant. He delights in enterprise and action, but to sustain him he needs a tranquil mind and a whole heart. He expends his moral force in the conflicts of the world. His feelings are easily lacerated to the utmost point of endurance by perpetual collision, irritation, and disappointment. To recover his equanimity aud composure, home must be to him a place of repose, of cheerfulness, of comfort ; and his soul renews its strength, and again goes forth with fresh vigor to encounter the labors and troubles of the world. But if at home ho finds no rest, and is there met by a bad temper, sullennoss, or gloom, or is assailed by discontent, oomplaint, and reproaches, the heart breaks, the spirits are crushed, hope vanishes,, and the man sinks in total despair. Let woman know, then,

that she ministers at the very fountain of life aud happiness. It is her hand that deals out, with overflowing cup, its soul-refreshing waters, or casts in the branch of bitterness, which makes them poison and death. Ilcr ardent spirit breathes the breath of life into all enterprise. Her pAtience and constancy are mainly instrumental in carrying forward to completion the best human designs. Her more delicate moral sensibility is the unseen power which is ever at work to purify and refine society. And the nearest glimpse of heaven that mortals ever get on earth is that domestic circle which her hands have trained to intelligence, virtue, and love, which her gentle influence pervades, and of which her radiant presence is the centre and the sun

The Cholera al Porto Rico ! ! ! We have been favored with the perusal of a private communication from Arecibo, Porto Rico, dated 13th Deer., from which we make the following extract in relation to the Epidemic now raging in that Island : þÿ C" " I mentioned the distressing news of the Cholera having appeared in our Island, and as we presume all of you will be uneasy of us I hasten to acquaint you that as yet the Epidemic lias not visited us, and consequently with thanks to our Maker can say we are in a healthy state. " The disease spreads rapidly, and sweeps otf the people as fast as it spreads. " Here we arc prepared with all that can be imagined to defend us of this enemy. " Up to the 8tb instant, in all the towns there have been 2989 cases and 1275 deaths þÿ excluding the city." Another letter from Ponce, dated the 10th instant, alluding to the Cholera, says: þÿ "I hardly think it will reach Ponce, as it has not as yet taken our direction. It appears very mild, for it has now been here one month, and I don't believe 500 persons have died from it up to date, although it lias visited 9 or 10 different villages. It appears that a bush we have by the name of the Guaco, lias proved to be an infallible cure ; on all the estates where it has been used hardly a single person died."

A mer i ca . From the. New York Herald , December 8. The intelligence from Antigua is highly important. It appears that the brig Loango, of Philadelphia, was boarded in the harbor of St. Johns, on the 10th ultimo, by the Superintendant of Police and Colonial Treasurer þÿ the orders of the English Governor þÿ who forcibly took away the cook, named John Ross, under the pretence of his being a slave anxious to "set his foot on British soil." In vain Ross protested that he was a free man. lie was dragged ashore, and himself and about one hundred and fifty dollars which he possessed placed in charge of his newly found friends. The British officials went on board the vessel under the miserable pretext of searching for articles contraband of w;ir. Ross was in custody of the police, awaiting the result of an investigation. Capt. Little, of the Loango, sends us a full statement of the case, which we hope will engage the greatest attention of the Cabinet at Washington.

CAPTAIN LITTLE'S STATEMENT. Antigua, Nov. 12, 1855. James Gordon Bennett, Esq. þÿ You will no doubt, on the arrival of the Sabine at your port, hear of the insult offered our flag on the 10th inst. The facts are as follows: þÿ The brig Loango, of and from Philadelphia, arrived here on the 6th inst., and on the 10th was boarded by the authorities, during my absence, under the pretence of searching for contraband goods. No search was made, but the Colonial Treasurer, Mr. Price, called the cook, told him he had understood he was a slave,

3 J>. ATI 3 and be had come on board to give him the protection which the British government held forth to the slave who arrived in their waters. Although the cook protested over and over again that he was a free man, he was by force removed on shore, and, with $150 in double eagles and some small gold, is now taken care of by his friends. I send you a copy of the Times, containing an article on the subject. The matter is now in the hands of Mr. Higinbotham, our Commercial Agent, who intends to see me through in my demand for satisfaction to the flag of which 1 was at that time the guardian. I will say, also that every merchant and others not connected with the government, declare the act to have been a most flagrant outrage to the American flag. The crew also were offered the glorious protection of British soil ; hut they told the officers they knew when they were well off. To Mr. Knox, of the firm of McDonald & Co. I am under great obligation for the manner in which he advocated my cause ; and I feel well satisfied that the insult to him and myself will he redressed, if it depends on his exertions. I am, dear sir, respectfully, your obedient servant, TIIOS. J. LITTLE, Master of the American brig Loango.

THE NEWSPAPER ACCOUNT. From the St. Johus Weekly Times, Nov. 10. It having been ascertained yesterday, that there was on board of the brigantine Loango, from Philadelphia, a fugitive slave by the name of John Ross, who was anxious to set his foot upon British soil, where the inestimable boon of freedom would be instantly realized, but who by some means was debarred from doing so although he offered five dollars for his conveyance ashore, the Superintendant of Police, Mr. Shoerdiche, was made acquainted with the circumstances, who, with his usual promptitude, as we are acting under told, associated himself with Mr. Price, the Colonial Treasurer ; and having obtained the sanction and authority of his excellency the Governor, at once removed the man from the vessel and placed him among freemen. VVe understand that the narrative of his escape from slavery is graphic and interesting. It may hereafter find a place in our columns. The man is now at the Police office pending an investigation into the circumstances, which we regret our inability to report in our present issue.
E u r o p e a n. From the London Weekly Despatch , December 2.

ENGLAND. The most important intelligence at the conclusion of the week is also the most welcome. There appears to be no longer any apprehension, on either side of the Atlantic, of war between England and America. There is a great deal of special pleading in the Government journals, the Post and the Globe, about the status of Colonel Turr, whom the British Government sent into Wallachia to buy horses for our public service. First, it is pleaded that he had no right to a General uniform ; then, that an English British

would probably have done what Coronini has done ; then that, although Wallachia is a Turkish province, Austria, among other powers, has a right, by treaty, to deal with its own subjects throughout Turkey. All this is canting, cowardly evasion. If we have the clear law with us so much the better; but this is certain, that any transgression of it is ours, not Turr's. We have adopted him as our servant ; he was in that character in the territory of our ally by our direction ; his offence against Austria was a political one, nothing more than keeping his oath to the Hungarian Constitu- O O tion, which a perjured Emperor and a treacherous Government enjoined him to swear. It Austria or its General believed in a right to claim and punish him, to do so was an insult to the Power that bad employed him. We might wrong engaging be in with him, wrong in sending him into Wallachia ; but he must not be proved to be wrong in trusting to our protection. Austria may give him up to us courteously, if she will ; if not, we must compel her, or avenge the victim our act has put in her power. Lord Palmerston cannot take too high a ground in this matter ; no, not if the consequence should be that Austria declares for Russia the next hour. We have not fallen so low as to let such a contemner strike us with impunity. We must not, in any such case, calculate chances ; we must feel that national character includes all ; that nothing can happen to us worse than to lose its integrity. As to what is pre-

paring for the Austrian empire within itself, we need ordy record that already several private Protestant schools are being closed in Hungary. If human nature is not some other thing in the Austrian dominions than what we recognise for it here, the Concordat has settled the destiny of that miserable State.

PRUSSIA. Berlin, November 20. The Chambers have just been opened by the King. The following is an extract from his Majesty's Speech : þÿ " Gentlemen, þÿ The conflict between several European Powers is not yet at an end. Our fatherland, however, continues to be the abode of peace. I trust in God that it will remain so, and that 1 shall succeed in preserving the honor and standing of Prussia without inflicting upon our country the heavy sacrifices of war. I am proud to say that 1 know of no people so well prepared for war, or more ready for sacrifices than my own whenever its honor or interests are really in danger. This proud consciousness, however, imposes upon me the duty, while abiding faithfully by obligations already contracted, not to enter into further engagements, the political and military liabilities of which are not to be estimated beforehand. In the attitude assumed by Prussia, Austria and Germany behold a valid security for the further maintenance of that independent position which is equally conducive to the attainment of an equitable and lasting peace and compatible with sincere good wishes for all."

THE SEA OF AZOFF. The following telegraphic dispatch from Sir E. Lyons has been received at the Admiralty : þÿ VARNA, November 18. Captain Sherard Osborn reports that on the 5th and 6th instant a flotilla, under his orders in the Sea of Azoff, destroyed enormous quantities of grain and forage, of this year's harvest, which was compactly stacked in six tiers, extending two miles along the coast near Gheisk Liman, ready to be conveyed, partly to the Crimean army, after the formation of the ice in the Sea of Azoff, and partly to the army of the Caucasus, and which ( the enemy thought secure from any naval attack. By the skill'ulness of the arrangements, and the manner in which they were executed by Captain Osborn, in which lie was ably assisted by Commander Kennedy, the enterprise was effected in the most brilliant manner, by landing on three points under cover of the gun-boats of the allies, in the face ot not less than 4,000 cavalry and infantry.

RUSSIA. The Paris Correspondent of the Times says: þÿ "The rumours which circulated some weeks ago, of a disposition on the part of the Russian Government to negotiate with a view to peace, are again revived in certain quarters, but, most probably, with as little foundation as they then had. Except that trustworthy intelligence from St. Petersburg and some other parts of Russia speaks of the desire of the commercial population for the termination of the war, I am acquainted with no data which would prove the fact. It is indeed, said that the experiment made at Kinhurn of the efficiency of the new floating batteries invented by the Emperor Louis Napoleon, in attacking, with comparative safety, the most formidable granite fortresses, has struck with dismay the heart of the Czar, and his advisers, and convinced him that the protection on which he lias hitherto relied at length begins to fail him. Hence it is conjectured that he feels that there is no alternative than to submit in time, or to see crumble before him the gigantic defences on the solidity of which the last hope of safety, if not of triumph, depends. The execution done by these new instruments of destruction, and the comparative impunity with which they have done their work, have no doubt, presented an unexpected feature in the war, and will compel the enemy to find out new means of defence that may postpone the catastrophe which is impending over him. From this, however, to suing for peace the distance is
great. Russia does not appear to be as yet exhausted. We may depend upon it the struggle is not yet over. Our enemy will not submit without another

effort. He will still endeavour to gather from every available quarter all that can add to the arts of destruction to counterbalance our superiority, and will combine all the materials of havoc within his reach before he comes as a suppliant acknowledging his defeat, and demanding mercy þÿ for to that point he must be reduced at last."

It is more appalling than any we recollect to have ever read in the history of these reptiles : Some time last summer the inhabitants of Manchester, Mississippi, gave a barbacue, which was attended by most of the fashion and beauty of the town and surrounding country. It happened that among the guests there was a young lady, Miss M., who Eastern cities, recently from one of the was on a visit to her relations in the neighbourhood of the town. Miss M. was a gay and extremely fashionable young lady, and withal possessed an uncommon share of spirit and courage, except in the matter of snakes, and of those she had so great a dread that she scarcely dared to walk any where except in the most frequented places, for fear of encountering them.

3 e at ir atiis, Every effort was used, but without avail, to rid her of her childish fears. They haunted her continually, until at last it became the settled conviction of her mind that she was destined to fall a victim to the fangs of a rattlesnake. The sequel will show how soon her terrible presentiment was fulfilled. Toward the close of the day, while scores of the fairy feet were keeping time in the dance to the music, and the whole company were in the full tide of enjoyment, a scream was heard from Miss M., followed by the most agonizing cries for help. The crowd gathered her instantly, and beheld her standing, the perfect image of despair, with her hands grasping a portion of her dress with all the tenacity of a vice. It was some time before she could be rendered sufficiently calm to tell the cause of her alarm, and then they gathered from her broken exclamations that she was grasping the head of a snake among the folds of her dress, and feared to let go her hold for fear of receiving the fatal blow. This intelligence caused many to shrink from her; but the ladies, for their honour be it told, determined not to leave her in her direful extremity. They besought her not to relax her hold, as safety depended upon it, until some one could be found with courage enough to seize and remove the terrible animal. There were none of the ladies willing, however, to perform the act, and the situation of Miss M., was becoming more and more critical every moment. It was evident that her strength

was falling fast, and that she could not maintain her hold many minutes longer. A hasty consultation among the calmest of the ladies was held, when it was determined that Dr. Tison, who was present, should be called to their assistance. He was quickly on the spot, and being a man of uncommon courage, he was not many minutes within the circle of weeping and half-fainting females until he caught the tail of the snake and wound it round his hand to make sure of his hold. He then told Miss M. that she must let go at the moment he jerked it away ; and to make the act as instantaneous as possible, he would pronounce the words, one, two, three, and at the moment he pronounced the and go her hold, last word she must let he doubted not he could withdraw the snake before it would have time to strike. All stood in breathless horror awaiting the act of life and death ; and at the moment the word three was pronounced the doctor jerked out the largest and most diabolical-looking bustle that was ever seen in Mississippi. The whole affair was then explained. The fastenings of the machine had become loose during dancing, and it had shifted its position in such a way that it dangled about the lady's limbs, and induced the belief that it was a snake with an enormous head. The docter fell right down in his tracks and fainted þÿ he did.

A Shifty Judge. þÿ A short time since they had a queer case of a Circuit Judge in the Western District of Tcnnesee. He was a good lawyer, and cared nothing for appearance and less for dress. The latter he knew nothing about, it being left entirely to Betty his wife. His Betty was absent from home once when he started round on his circuit, leaving the Judge to pack his clothes for the trip. He did so, but instead of finding his shirts he seized on a pile of his wife's what-you-call-ems, used for a like purpose. A learned brother, who

roomed with him, was much amused a few mornings afterward at the queer appearance of the Judge, nothing being in sight but his head, arms and feet, his looks of bewilderment, and his sotto voce reflections, which were : " I wonder what on earth made Betty cut off my shirt-sleeves? I don't see!" It is probable that he heard the reason the next time lie saw Betty, but not before, as the bar kept dark on the matter that round. We think he had a very poor knowledge of the chemise-try, as an applied science. From the London Weekly Despatch, November 25. The in" ws positively asserted by the Paris correspondent of t lie Times , that General Oanrobert has concluded an alliance, offensive and defensive, between France and Sweden þÿ that the Swedish and Norwegian gun-boats are to operate with our fleets next Spring þÿ and that a a view of raising Poland is, to use the landing is to be made in þÿ Courland, with most hackneyed of all trite phrases, yet the most applicable in this case, "most important, if true." The Times, we perceive, reiterates its assertion, includes Denmark in the treaty, and insists that Prussia is already alarmed, and presses upon Russia to conclude a peace. The results of General Canrobert's mission, it appears to us, must remain a mystery, because they must be in the conditional mood, future tense. If Sweden, Norway and Denmark intend fully to join the Western Powers in the spring, they cannot say so even to their proposed allies. They can allow the purpose to be half seen, guessed at þÿ that is the utmost. The reign of winter, ice, darkness, and Russia is at hand for three or four months in the Baltic regions. It would he a throwing away of strength to challenge the Northern bear in his own congenial season. Scandinavia must wait for the sun, or tight at disadvantage or at much expense to France and England. With the mortar arid gun-boats, and, as we trust, floating batteries, which England and France may, in all common Nense, be presumed to be building, the Norwegian, Danish and Swedish flotil-

a vr. e at i a: yt i a. our Consul iu the Wallachian capital, it is most probable that we should have had to add that he had been shot. Mr. Colquhoun saw the Austrian General, and put it to him on his " responsibility" not to injure a man in the British service. The Austrian claims the right to seize his deserter wherever he finds him, and declares that he will break his sword if his Government orders that Turr shall be given up. Thus the intemperate Commander has pledged himself as fully and as offensively as possible ; and it may really becorno incumbent upon the Austrian Government to accept his resignation, in order to do justice to Great Britain The fact is, that Turr is a Hungarian, a refugee from his country, and has been employed by us to buy horses in VVallachia. Now, in Wallachia it is for Coronini to remember that he has no jurisdiction whatever, that his armed force gives him no rightful authority over anythiug but itself ; that he is a guest iu the Turkish dominions, and that Turr, while in them, is the commissioned officer of Turkey's ally the Queen of Great Britain. On her behalf he went to Bucharest, and the last pound and the last man of this empire are pledged for his safety, his honourable treatment as one of ourselves. We have to teach the Austrian braggadocio, and, if necessary, his master, to respect the rights of nations. We have to show Austria þÿ the thing we call Austria for want of a better word, the Hapsburg dynasty that rules over so many unwilling races þÿ that the holding of the Principali-

ties is no possession, that they are still Turkey's þÿ that Europe will preserve them for her and for their inhabitants þÿ and that any assumption out of the Austrian empire of authority over men admitted to British rights, still more invested with British office, is a national quarrel There is little love lost, doubtless, between Austrian officers, or the Austrian Court, and the British people. They may hate our principles as utterly as we despise theirB but if there be any polititcal reason why the two countries should remain at peace, it will be absolutely necessary that no Austrian shall in any ease usurp a privilege against us, or lift a finger against any thing or person that we own. Count Coronini may, perhaps, repent of his arrogance and rashness ; else, should his Government refuse to reverse the consequences of his doings, or should he in any wise make them irreversible, it will be time to show that absulutism has not deprived us of our old island pretensions, that we will neither hush up wrongs nor shrink from any responsibility in making their doers repent of them. Perhaps this occurrence may bring a speedier deliverance to tbo Principalities: if so, Austria will be struck in the right place : a great good will result from the evil, should an injury offered to the powerful end in removing a bitter tyranny from the necks of the weak.

Town Talk. In a recent number of the North British Revitw, an eminent English author recorded the opinions of a most competent witness on the military qualities of different nations. A Polish General who had fought under Diebitsch and against Paskiewitch þÿ the veteran who was defeated at the head of the Piedmontese army by Radetzky at Novara þÿ after assigning their proper places, according to his opinion, to Russians, Germans and Frenchmen, has deolared his conviotion that the Turk is the best soldier in the world next to tho Englishman ; and he adds that the Turk is always sober. During the present war no Russian troops have ever defeated an equal number of Ottomans, except in the Asiatio battles of last year, where observers always attributed the result to the gross incapacity of the

Generals. At Kars, however, the Turks had the advantage of an English commander, ably supported by General Kmety, as well as by his own officers ; on the iDgour they were led by the General who already, in the Principalities, had given proof both of skilful strategy and prudent daring ; and on both occasions they have, as in the Tanubian campaign of 1853, shown their su periority to the Russians, it will be an unpardonable error if the allies fail to profit by the lesson We are too apt to forget that the l urks have again and again thundered at the gates of Vienna, and their success at Silistria, Kars and Ingour proves that their mettle is as high as ever. In fact, let the Western Powers put the Sultan in the way of correcting the evils of mal-administration, and the Turks will yet prove that alone they are more than a match for the Russians. The new doctrine of Muridism, which is that all Mahometans should combine under one ruler, is spreading fast, and may again make the Sultan the most powerful monarch in the world. An improvement has been shown at the French Exhibition in lucifer matches. The two inflammable ingredients, which together are required to make up the ignition of the match, are now separated. One part is retained in the match, the other lodged in the sand paper on which the match is rubbed. This greatly adds to the safety of the use of this convenience A letter from Vienna states : þÿ It is not doubted here that Russia will well employ the winter months, and bring a tremen-

dous army into the field next spring, but it is considered morally certain that she will yield to the force of circumstances should she be as unfortunate during the next campaign as she has been during the present. A person whoso basis in favour of Russia is notorious, yesterday confessed to me that his friends wore sadly afflicted Pacha. " It is no disgrace," said he, at the news of the victory gained by Omer " to be beaten by English and French troops ; but it is humiliating in the extreme to be worsted by Turkish hordes commanded by an Austian renegade. The defeat at Kars was bad enough, but the fact that the Russians were driven from their fortified position on the left bank of the Ingour by the Turks, is positively disgraceful." þÿ London Weekly Dispatch
